title: Cap. X Ultimum Prima: early anti-Pelagian councils did not expressly define absolute predestination — yet defined much that cannot stand if absolute gratuitous predestination is overturned; Faustus condemned
pass_a_gloss: First, we confess that the Councils which were celebrated against Pelagius and the Semipelagians in Augustine’s own times, or in the age next after his death—such as were Diospolis, Milevis, Carthage, Orange, and some others—did not expressly, directly and particularly sanction the doctrine of absolute predestination, or condemn the contrary opinion of election and reprobation from foresight of diverse acts in men. Yet this we affirm, that in these Councils many things were defined which cannot stand if absolute and gratuitous predestination be overturned, or if that conditioned election and preterition be laid down which Faustus, and after him some others, and at length Arminius undertook to cultivate and defend. Hither also it comes that Faustus’s books, in which he laboriously tries to establish that conditioned election and to explode the absolute, were condemned by the ancient Church, as is clear from Gratian, Distinct. 15. The Decree stands in the Tom. of Councils, and was sanctioned by Gelasius in a Synod of seventy Bishops. Hormisdas also, consulted concerning Faustus’s book, answers that Catholic doctrine ought to be learned from Augustine and Prosper, not likewise from Faustus.
pass_b_english: First we confess: the councils against Pelagius and the Semipelagians in Augustine’s time or the age just after his death—Diospolis, Milevis, Carthage, Orange, and others—did not expressly, directly, and particularly sanction absolute predestination or condemn foresight-election and reprobation. Yet we affirm that much defined in those councils cannot stand if absolute gratuitous predestination is overturned, or if that conditioned election and preterition is set up which Faustus, then others, and at last Arminius undertook to cultivate and defend. Add that Faustus’s books, which labor to fix conditioned election and explode the absolute, were condemned by the ancient church—clear from Gratian, Distinctio 15; the decree stands in the councils’ Tomus, sanctioned by Gelasius in a synod of seventy bishops. Hormisdas, asked about Faustus’s book, answers that catholic doctrine should be learned from Augustine and Prosper, not from Faustus.
source_text: Primo, fatemur, Concilia quae celebrata fuerunt contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos ipsius Augustini temporibus, aut saeculo ab obitu ejus proximo, qualia fuerunt Diospolitanum, Milevitanum, Carthaginense, Arausicanum, aliaque nonnulla, non expresse, directe et particulariter sanxisse doctrinam de absoluta praedestinatione, aut condemnasse opinionem contrariam de electione et reprobatione ex praevisione diversorum actuum in hominibus. Illud tamen affirmamus, in hisce Conciliis multa fuisse definita quae stare non possunt absoluta et gratuita praedestinatione eversa, aut posita illa conditionata electione et praeteritione quam Faustus, et post illum alii nonnulli, ac tandem Arminius excolendam et defendendam susceperunt. Huc accedit, Fausti libros in quibus conditionatam illam electionem operose stabilire conatur, et absolutam explodere, damnatos fuisse ab antiqua Ecclesia, ut ex Gratiano liquet, Distinct. 15. Decretum extat a Tom. Conciliorum, et sancitum fuit a Gelasio in Synodo septuaginta Episcoporum. Hormisda etiam de Fausti libro consultus respondet, Doctrinam Catholicam ex Augustino et Prospero, non item e Fausto, disci oportere.
